tldr: We propose a unified framework that enables humanoid robots to master visual whole-body loco-manipulation without large-scale teleoperation data or task-specific reward engineering, achieved by mimicking synthetic trajectories generated from LLM-crafted motion templates.
hero_caption: Overview of SUGARv2. On the left, reusable task templates generated by an LLM (GPT-6 Astra) are adapted to various spatial configurations ($c_1$–$c_4$) to synthesize interaction references. On the right, a privileged teacher policy is trained using a shared reference-based mimic reward across all tasks, and then distilled into a visual student policy alongside reinforcement learning (RL).
overview:
Humanoid loco-manipulation—walking around while picking up and carrying objects—is a major dream of robotics, but it has long faced massive hurdles in data collection and reward engineering. Collecting real-world teleoperation demonstrations is labor-intensive, and manually crafting reward functions for each individual task simply does not scale.

To overcome this, the authors developed "SUGARv2," a unified framework that tackles these issues through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. First, an LLM is used to create reusable task templates defining contact orders and motion sequences. These templates are then geometrically adapted to the initial spatial configurations of the robot and objects, automatically synthesizing smooth whole-body robot motions and object trajectories. During the policy learning stage, a shared reference-based "mimic reward" is set to imitate these synthesized trajectories. A privileged teacher policy with access to full ground-truth states (such as precise 3D object coordinates) is trained first. Then, this knowledge is distilled into a visual policy that only takes egocentric camera images and proprioception (joint angles, etc.) as inputs, further refined via reinforcement learning.

Evaluated on five simulated humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieved an average success rate of 91.0%, outperforming existing baselines by over 50 percentage points. Furthermore, policies trained entirely in simulation were deployed zero-shot onto a real humanoid robot (Unitree G1), successfully demonstrating seamless coordination of walking, squatting, and carrying.
contributions: Proposed a pipeline that adapts LLM-generated reusable task templates to diverse spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated whole-body motions, object trajectories, and contact labels at low cost without human teleoperation.

Constructed a unified learning framework that defines a shared reference-based mimic reward across all tasks, consistently covering privileged teacher training, visual student distillation, and reinforcement learning.

Achieved an average success rate of 91.0% across five humanoid whole-body tasks, demonstrating generalization to unseen backgrounds and object instances, as well as zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree G1 robot.

sections.heading: Freeing Humanoids from Manual Data Collection and Reward Design
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation has been hard to scale because expanding to new tasks and spatial configurations required manual teleoperation and customized reward design. SUGARv2 acquires diverse visual whole-body skills at low cost by combining template-based reference synthesis with a task-agnostic imitation learning pipeline.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to operate effectively in the real world, visual whole-body loco-manipulation—coordinating two-handed manipulation while maintaining bipedal balance—is essential. However, training visual policies for these skills typically imposes enormous human effort whenever tasks or object configurations change.

Existing approaches suffer from two main bottlenecks. The first is data collection cost. While methods like HumanoidMimicGen can automatically expand teleoperated demonstrations, they still require initial human demonstrations and struggle with coordination because upper-body manipulation and lower-body locomotion are planned separately. Meanwhile, approaches like GRAIL that extract motions from video generative models require heavy video generation and pose estimation per configuration, often leading to physically inaccurate contacts. The second bottleneck is training design cost. Reinforcement learning methods demand delicate task-specific reward engineering, making it difficult to scale across diverse tasks.

To break through these challenges, the authors propose SUGARv2 with two core components. First, a large language model (GPT-6 Astra) creates reusable task templates specifying contact schedules and relative poses, which are geometrically adapted to diverse initial configurations to automatically synthesize coordinated robot and object trajectories. Second, a shared reference-based mimic reward is used within a physics simulator to train a privileged teacher policy, followed by distillation and reinforcement learning into a visual student policy within the exact same pipeline. This minimizes both manual demonstration collection and task-specific reward engineering.

captions.F2: Overall framework of SUGARv2. The left side synthesizes interaction references for various spatial configurations from task templates, while the right side uses a shared mimic reward for privileged teacher training, visual policy distillation, and RL.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Synthetic Data, Mimic Control, and Visual Policies
sections.summary: Prior works have independently advanced synthetic demonstration generation, physics-based motion tracking, and visual reinforcement learning. SUGARv2 unifies these areas, achieving visual humanoid loco-manipulation through template-based geometric reference synthesis and a shared imitation learning formulation.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans three main domains:

### Policy Learning from Synthetic Demonstrations
Methods like MimicGen geometrically transform existing demonstrations to generate synthetic robot trajectories. However, when applied to humanoids, many decouple locomotion and manipulation, compromising natural whole-body coordination. On the other hand, generative-model approaches like GRAIL synthesize motions via video generation, but they suffer from high computational overhead and frequent contact misalignment with objects. SUGARv2 overcomes this by adapting keyframes with explicit contact semantics to spatial configurations and using a conditional motion generation model, producing physically plausible references with high efficiency.

### Motion Tracking and Interaction Mimicking
Techniques for reproducing kinematic references in physics simulation have matured in character animation and locomotion control. Object-centric imitation frameworks (such as SkillMimic and InterMimic) demonstrated that defining mimic rewards over both robot and object motions eliminates the need for manual task-specific reward engineering. SUGARv2 pushes this concept further, applying a unified imitation objective to the challenging problem of whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation.

### Visual Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Learning visual policies that directly drive whole-body motions from camera inputs typically relies on imitation learning from teleoperation or reinforcement learning (RL). In RL, teacher-student frameworks (such as VIRAL) that first train a privileged teacher and then distill it into a visual student are effective; however, they conventionally require task-specific reward engineering for the teacher. SUGARv2 drastically reduces this task-level tuning burden by using synthetic references and a shared mimic reward across all tasks.

sections.heading: A Two-Stage Pipeline: Weaving Trajectories from Templates, Distilling from Teachers to Vision
sections.summary: SUGARv2 consists of two stages: interaction reference synthesis and policy learning. Task templates from an LLM are adapted to spatial configurations to produce whole-body references, and a privileged teacher trained with a shared mimic reward is distilled and refined into a visual policy via RL.
sections.details:
The proposed approach trains a task-specific policy that takes egocentric RGB images and proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) as inputs to coordinate whole-body joints and complete each task.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Framework Overview
The overall system operates in two stages, as illustrated in Fig. F2. The first stage synthesizes whole-body robot motions, object trajectories, and contact labels tailored to spatial configurations. The second stage uses these references to train a privileged teacher and then transfers that expertise to a visual policy via distillation and RL.

### 3.2 Interaction Reference Synthesis
Trajectory synthesis begins with GPT-6 Astra creating a task template $\mathcal{T}$. The template specifies a sequence of key whole-body poses, robot-object spatial relationships, and hand-object contact labels (Section 3.2.1).
Next, the template is adapted (instantiated) according to the initial object locations and goal configurations $c$ (Section 3.2.2). The system accounts for object symmetry, reachability, and stance locations that minimize base movement to determine keyframes, then interpolates between them using a conditional motion generation model to produce smooth whole-body motions. Object trajectories are geometrically derived from hand motions, resulting in a complete reference trajectory $\tau_c$ with robot joint trajectories $q_t^{\mathrm{robot}}$, object trajectories $q_t^{\mathrm{obj}}$, and contact labels $l_t$ (see Fig. F3).

### 3.3 Policy Learning
In the policy learning stage, a shared mimic reward is used across all tasks. This reward comprises reference tracking terms, relative pose and contact matching terms, and regularization terms for smoothness and keeping objects within the camera field of view.
First, a privileged teacher policy driving a frozen, pretrained whole-body controller (WBC) is trained using PPO (Section 3.3.1). The teacher receives privileged state observations and interaction references, outputting WBC latent commands $z_t$ and gripper opening/closing commands $h_t$.
Next, the visual policy is trained (Section 3.3.2). Consisting of a pretrained visual encoder and an MLP, it predicts $(z_t, h_t)$ directly from egocentric camera images and proprioception. Training is conducted end-to-end, jointly optimizing a distillation loss (matching the teacher's actions on student-visited states) and a PPO loss using the shared mimic reward. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. F4, object textures, backgrounds, lighting, and camera poses are randomized online (domain randomization) in simulation, fostering robust visual representations for sim-to-real transfer.

captions.F3: Synthesized reference trajectories across five tasks. Colors darken as time progresses. Complex, coordinated whole-body motions are automatically generated, including tabletop pickup, floor-to-table placement, box carrying, and basket transport.
captions.F4: Examples of visual domain randomization applied during visual policy training. For the same robot pose, backgrounds, table textures, and object colors/shapes are varied to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Achieving a 91% Success Rate and Successful Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluated across five whole-body tasks, SUGARv2 achieved an average success rate of 91.0%, surpassing baselines by over 50 percentage points. Reference synthesis was roughly 90x faster than prior work, and zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree G1 succeeded.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluation was conducted on five tasks demanding high coordination between upper and lower body: Tabletop Pickup, Floor-to-Table, Same-Table, Box Carrying, and Basket Transport. For each task, 100 reference trajectories were synthesized to train corresponding visual policies. Baselines included imitation learning methods VIRAL and GR00T N1.7, as well as GRAIL for reference generation comparison.

### 4.2 Visual Policy Performance and Generalization
In simulation, SUGARv2 outperformed all baselines across all five tasks, achieving an average success rate of 91.0%. It surpassed the strongest baseline, VIRAL (39.6% average), by a substantial 51.4 percentage points. In zero-shot generalization tests with unseen background textures and novel intra-category object instances, performance dropped only slightly, confirming robust visual generalization.

### 4.3 Reference Quality and Synthesis Efficiency
Compared to video-generation-based GRAIL, which took an average of 36.1 minutes to generate one valid trajectory, SUGARv2 required just 0.4 minutes (about 24 seconds)—a ~90x speedup. Moreover, because GRAIL trajectories often contained physical inconsistencies, the teacher tracking error was high; in contrast, references from SUGARv2 yielded significantly lower tracking errors and markedly higher success rates for the downstream visual policy.

### 4.4 Reference Dataset Size and Ablations
Varying the number of synthesized trajectories from 20 to 500 showed steady performance gains up to 100 trajectories, after which gains plateaued. Thus, 100 trajectories was chosen as the optimal cost-performance balance.
Ablation studies also revealed that both teacher distillation and mimic-reward RL are indispensable. Relying solely on RL from scratch without distillation resulted in nearly 0% success, while distillation alone without RL fine-tuning led to a severe drop in success rate.

### 4.6 Real Humanoid Validation (Sim-to-Real)
The visual policy trained entirely in simulation was deployed zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot. As shown in Fig. F6, the robot stably performed complex sequences including squatting to pick up objects from the floor and carrying boxes with both hands while walking. Observed failure cases typically stemmed from missing recovery behaviors: when an initial grasp failed, the robot lacked retry motions and proceeded with the transport phase with empty hands.

captions.F6: Real humanoid robot (Unitree G1) experiments. Guided by first-person camera views (top-right inset), the robot smoothly executes whole-body motions including crouching, grasping objects, walking while carrying, and placing.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Stepping Stones Toward General Multitask VLA Models
sections.summary: SUGARv2 demonstrates low-cost acquisition of diverse humanoid loco-manipulation skills by pairing LLM-assisted template adaptation with task-agnostic imitation learning. Future work aims to expand toward long-horizon compound tasks and multitask VLA models.
sections.details:
This study presented SUGARv2, a unified framework for scaling visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition.

Instead of relying on human teleoperation data or task-specific reward tuning, SUGARv2 establishes a coherent pipeline: building reusable task templates with an LLM, geometrically synthesizing reference trajectories, and training policies via privileged teacher learning followed by visual student distillation plus RL using a shared mimic reward. This approach proves that high simulation success rates (91.0%) and smooth real-robot transfer can be achieved with minimal human effort.

The authors note current limitations: reference synthesis is currently restricted to relatively clean environments and short-horizon interactions. Moving forward, they plan to extend the synthesis pipeline to cluttered environments and longer-horizon tasks, transitioning from individual task-specific policies to a unified multitask Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model capable of executing diverse interactions from language instructions.

takeaways: Decoupling coarse sequence definition (via LLM templates) from physically and geometrically constrained motion interpolation allows fast, low-cost synthesis (0.4 min per trajectory) of physically plausible whole-body references at scale.

Instead of manually engineering task-specific reward functions, defining a shared mimic reward over synthesized robot and object trajectories enables learning diverse tasks within a single, uniform RL pipeline.

A hybrid design that provides a solid initial visual policy via privileged teacher distillation while continuing mimic RL under the teacher's behavioral guidance is critical for mastering challenging visuomotor skills.
limitations: Recovery behaviors are currently lacking when initial grasps fail; the robot tends to proceed through subsequent carrying motions even with empty hands.

Reference synthesis is currently demonstrated on short-horizon motions in simplified scenes, posing challenges for scaling to heavily cluttered environments with dense furniture or long-horizon tasks.
Because separate visual policies are trained for each task, integrating these capabilities into a single multitask VLA model that responds to diverse language instructions remains future work.
